# FinFAIR: Reprex applications

## Introduction

Heritage Digital Twins require more than semantic descriptions of cultural heritage objects. They must support the continuing production, review, maintenance and governance of knowledge derived from heterogeneous documentary evidence. In practice, this knowledge is maintained across institutional databases, knowledge graphs, archival systems and research workflows that cannot reasonably be expected to adopt a single ontology or software environment.

The [Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space (FUDSS)](https://finnougric.net/) addresses this challenge through an operational architecture combining Wikibase for collaborative knowledge maintenance, Betwixt for provenance-aware knowledge production and review, Apache Jena Fuseki for semantic querying, and Sampo-UI for exploration. Rather than replacing these applications with an HDT-O-specific repository, we propose projecting their maintained knowledge into ontology-aligned representations suitable for exchange with ECHOES.

Our contribution is threefold. First, we demonstrate how existing Wikibase resources can be represented as Heritage Digital Twins (`HC2`) while preserving the distinction between the twins and their represented heritage entities (`HC1`). Second, we propose a workflow connecting reviewed propositions and their provenance to persistent Heritage Proposition Sets (`HC16`). Third, we investigate how documentary works and their digital representations can be independently identified and governed, particularly when rights and permitted uses differ across representations.

Using the **Dēliņi farmhouse and its photographic documentation** as a worked example, this paper presents reproducible RDF representations and identifies both proposed solutions and unresolved questions concerning HDT-O modelling, persistence, provenance and interoperability. Its purpose is to establish a concrete basis for technical discussion, validation and potential collaborative development with ECHOES, rather than to claim conformance with an exchange specification that has not yet been fully established.

The **Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space (FUDSS)** is a governed cultural heritage data sharing environment built around four complementary applications. Each supports a different aspect of creating, maintaining, reviewing, querying, and sharing knowledge about Heritage Digital Twins[^1].

[^1]: See *Federating Open Knowledge through Wikibase: The Case of The Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space* [@fudss_2026]

### MediaWiki and Wikibase

We use **MediaWiki and Wikibase** as a collaborative, user-friendly knowledge management environment. Wikibase stores structured statements in a relational database (MariaDB or MySQL) and exposes them as a document-oriented knowledge graph through RDF and SPARQL interfaces.

Wikibase is the software underlying Wikidata, one of the world's largest collaboratively maintained knowledge graphs. Its familiar item-and-property model allows researchers and curators to maintain semantic data without requiring detailed knowledge of RDF or ontology engineering.

Our Wikibase implementation supports bounded federation with Wikidata, Wikimedia Commons, and Wikipedia, allowing locally governed knowledge to be connected to external authority records, media resources, and encyclopaedic descriptions.

### Sampo-UI

**Sampo-UI** is a semantic browsing framework developed at Aalto University and the University of Helsinki. It provides an established approach to exploring humanities knowledge graphs through dynamic faceted search, filtering, and visualisation.

In our implementation, Sampo-UI allows users to query and investigate multimodal heritage knowledge through intuitive interfaces, including tabular views and other projections of the underlying graph.

### Apache Jena Fuseki

**Apache Jena Fuseki** provides our SPARQL query service and API access to the semantic knowledge graph.

It serves as the query backend for our Sampo-UI application and enables authorised users and applications to access the graph programmatically through SPARQL endpoints.

### Betwixt

**Betwixt** is an intermediate representation framework and supporting reference application under development by Reprex. It facilitates the transformation, review, and exchange of semantic knowledge across different data structures, including knowledge graphs, relational databases, spreadsheets, tabular datasets, matrices, tensors, and vector representations.

Betwixt supports bounded federation between independently governed datasets and enables researchers and curators to work with graph-based knowledge without directly manipulating RDF.

For example, users can review, correct, or contribute candidate statements through familiar Excel spreadsheets or tabular HTML interfaces. These changes can be accompanied by provenance and review information before accepted propositions are incorporated into the knowledge graph.

### Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space

Together, these four applications provide the operational environment of the **Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space**.

Wikibase supports collaborative knowledge maintenance; Sampo-UI supports exploration and investigation; Fuseki provides semantic query and API services; and Betwixt supports cross-format knowledge exchange, curatorial review, and governed contributions.

**These applications are not themselves the Heritage Digital Twins or the underlying datasets.** They are complementary interfaces and services through which users interact with the knowledge maintained in the data sharing space. Our operational data model is designed to work effectively across these applications while supporting projection into ontology-aligned exchange representations, including HDT-O and CIDOC CRM.

In this document, we refer to a few digital twins developed in the *Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space*.

The [Dēliņi farmhouse (Q7328)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7328) is part of the [Dēliņi farmstead (Q5582)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q5582). Two historical photographs, [frontal view with well (Q7362)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7362) and [oblique view (Q7363)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7363), depict the farmhouse. Each photograph may have its own digital twin (`HC2`), while its digital image may also serve as a digital representation (`HC5`) of the farmhouse.

## Wikibase and Betwixt as operational semantic layers

Our applications use formal semantic models that serve a different purpose from domain ontologies such as HDT-O, CIDOC CRM, the International Council on Archives Records in Contexts Ontology (RiC-O) and DCTERMS[^2].

[^2]: International Council on Archives Records in Contexts Ontology (ICA RiC-O) version 1.1 [@RiC-O_1_1] and the library standard DCTERMS [@dublin_core_dcmi_2020].

These domain ontologies and vocabularies describe cultural heritage objects, archival records, bibliographic resources, their relationships, and their contexts. By contrast, Wikibase and Betwixt provide *operational semantic structures* that help us maintain, exchange, review, and investigate knowledge expressed using different domain models.

The [Wikibase ontology](https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Wikibase/DataModel) describes how knowledge is represented within the Wikibase data model, including items, properties, statements, qualifiers, references, and ranks [@wikibase_datamodel]. It enables us to maintain knowledge from different domains in a common, user-friendly environment while preserving mappings to the original domain ontologies.

The [Betwixt Vocabulary](https://usebetwixt.com/articles/betwixt-vocabulary.html), building on Schema.org and PROV-O, supports the intermediate representation and review of knowledge [@antal_betwixt_2026]. [Schema.org](https://schema.org/) provides a widely adopted vocabulary for structured data, while [PROV-O](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-o/) expresses the W3C PROV Data Model ([PROV-DM](https://www.w3.org/TR/prov-dm/)) for describing entities, activities, agents and their relationships in the production of information. Betwixt supports the transformation of statements from knowledge graphs, relational databases and other data structures into tabular, matrix, tensor or simpler graph representations. Researchers and curators can inspect, correct and warrant claims through familiar interfaces, such as Excel spreadsheets or HTML tables, before accepted knowledge is published back into a graph.

![Betwixt helps to retain the provenance of curatorial reviews of data ingested or modified into the digital twins.](images/prov/prov_delini.png){fig-align="center"}

The Wikibase ontology and Betwixt Vocabulary therefore support applications for data stewards, researchers and educators who possess expertise in cultural heritage but may lack specialised knowledge of RDF, ontology engineering or data programming. For example, a curator can describe the Dēliņi farmhouse in Wikibase, review candidate statements through Betwixt, investigate the resulting knowledge through Sampo-UI and query it through Apache Jena Fuseki. When interoperability requires an explicit HDT-O and CIDOC CRM representation, documented semantic mappings can produce the corresponding exchange structure.

**Our objective is to separate expertise in cultural heritage from expertise in semantic technologies.** Curators, researchers and community experts should be able to contribute and review knowledge using familiar applications, while the underlying semantic infrastructure supports provenance, governance and interoperability across different cultural heritage domains.

### Semantic projection from Wikibase to HDT-O

Wikibase can represent knowledge expressed in HDT-O and CIDOC CRM using its own item-and-property model (see [@pfeiffer_representing_2021; @kesaniemi_wb_cidoc_2022]). Ontology classes can be represented as Wikibase items and ontology properties as Wikibase properties. Class hierarchies can be expressed through *subclass of* relationships, while individual resources can be assigned to classes through *instance of* relationships. Wikibase statements can also carry qualifiers and references. However, representing an ontology within Wikibase and exporting an ontology-aligned RDF graph are distinct operations: the latter requires explicit mappings between Wikibase identifiers and the corresponding ontology classes, properties and relationships.

Our approach distinguishes the *operational representation of heritage knowledge* from its *ontology-aligned exchange representation*. Wikibase allows curators to work with familiar domain-specific classifications and maintain practical descriptions of heritage objects, while documented mappings allow us to project this knowledge into the more explicit conceptual structures of HDT-O and CIDOC CRM[^3]. The operational model does not need to reproduce every ontological distinction as a separately maintained Wikibase item, provided that these distinctions can be reconstructed without ambiguity when required for interoperability.

[^3]: Heritage Digital Twins Ontology [@echoes_hdto_1-1] and the CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model [@cidoc_2024].

In the Finno-Ugric Data Sharing Space, curators generally work with one principal Wikibase item for each heritage object or subject of documentation. This item serves as an operational shorthand for descriptions that HDT-O distinguishes between a Heritage Entity (`HC1`) and its Heritage Digital Twin (`HC2`). It combines statements about the represented entity with information about its classification, relationships, documentation and supporting evidence. For example, the [Dēliņi farmhouse (Q7328)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7328) and [Dēliņi farmstead (Q5582)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q5582) are maintained as operational digital twins, while also carrying statements that, in a fully articulated HDT-O representation, concern the underlying heritage entities.

This shorthand does not imply that the heritage entity and its digital twin are ontologically identical. Rather, the operational Wikibase item provides a convenient point of access to information that can be attributed to distinct `HC1` and `HC2` resources. We do not systematically create and populate both resources as separate user-facing records, because doing so would introduce additional curatorial work, redundancy and complexity without necessarily improving the everyday management of heritage knowledge. Where the distinction can be established unambiguously, however, the corresponding resources and relationships can be made explicit through semantic projection. The operational representation is therefore deliberately less explicit than the exchange representation, but not intended to contradict it.

To demonstrate this distinction, we also created the [physical Dēliņi farmhouse (Q7376)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7376) and [physical Dēliņi farmstead (Q7379)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7379) as separate `HC1` resources. These are connected to their respective digital twins through the Wikibase properties [has digital twin (P484)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Property:P484) and its inverse [digital twin of (P482)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Property:P482). The local Wikibase item [Q7377](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q7377) represents the `HC1 Heritage Entity` class. These additional records make explicit a distinction that would otherwise remain implicit in the operational descriptions.

The essential operational relationships can be illustrated as follows:

```{text}
PREFIX wd:  <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/>
PREFIX wdt: <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/>

# Physical farmhouse and its digital twin
wd:Q7376 wdt:P484 wd:Q7328 .
wd:Q7328 wdt:P482 wd:Q7376 .

# Physical farmstead and its digital twin
wd:Q7379 wdt:P484 wd:Q5582 .
wd:Q5582 wdt:P482 wd:Q7379 .
```

These explicitly modelled `HC1` resources demonstrate that Wikibase can represent the distinction between a heritage entity and its digital twin without requiring a different technical platform. Nevertheless, we regard this as an optional elaboration of the operational model rather than a requirement for every curatorial record. A curator describing the farmhouse generally intends to document the physical building, even though the statements are maintained in a digital information system. Requiring the curator to navigate and maintain two parallel descriptions would often add little practical value. The distinction becomes important when the information is interpreted according to an ontology that assigns different properties and relationships to the heritage entity and its digital twin.

![A building in an open-air museum is itself often a "physical twin" of a cultural heritage building or structure. For the user of our digital twins, it is clear that they are not inspecting the original farmhouse, which was relocated to the open air museum in 1971, and not the carefully maintained phyiscal heritage objects and structures, but its digital twin.](images/digital_twin/delini_digital_twin_slide_simplified.png){fig-align="center"}

Our preferred approach is therefore to preserve the established operational identifiers and treat their descriptions as shorthand for the corresponding ontological structures. In an HDT-O-aligned projection, the operational Wikibase item can retain its identity as the `HC2` digital twin, while the represented `HC1` heritage entity is made explicit. The projection may reuse existing `HC1` identifiers, as in this example, or materialise the corresponding resources through documented mappings. This allows the exchange representation to distinguish the physical heritage entities from their digital twins without requiring all such distinctions to be separately maintained in the operational application.

The projection must also account for differences between statements about the operational digital twin and statements about the heritage entity it represents. For example, the operational Wikibase item for the farmhouse records that it is heritage of the [Livonians (Q46)](https://reprexbase.eu/fu/Item:Q46), using the local property `P480`:

```{text}
PREFIX wd:  <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/>
PREFIX wdt: <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/prop/direct/>

wd:Q46 wdt:P14 wd:Q33 .
wd:Q7328 wdt:P480 wd:Q46 .
```

In the operational representation, this statement is attached to the principal Wikibase item because that item serves as the curator's point of access to the farmhouse description. In an HDT-O-aligned representation, however, the heritage relationship concerns the physical farmhouse (`HC1`), rather than its digital twin (`HC2`). The semantic projection therefore attributes the relationship to the corresponding heritage entity while preserving the identity of the operational digital twin:

```{text}
@prefix wd:  <https://reprexbase.eu/fu/entity/> .
@prefix hdt: <https://example.org/hdto/> .
@prefix crm: <http://www.cidoc-crm.org/cidoc-crm/> .

wd:Q7376
    a hdt:HC1, crm:E24_Physical_Human-Made_Thing ;
    hdt:HP1 wd:Q7328 ;
    hdt:HP15 wd:Q46 .

wd:Q7328
    a hdt:HC2 .

wd:Q46
    a crm:E74_Group .
```

The `hdt:` namespace in this illustrative excerpt is a placeholder pending alignment with the authoritative ontology release. The example demonstrates that semantic projection involves more than renaming Wikibase properties. The original statement `Q7328 → P480 → Q46` is interpreted as a heritage relationship between the physical farmhouse (`Q7376`) and the Livonians (`Q46`), while `HP1` explicitly connects the heritage entity to its digital twin. The operational statement is not treated as an erroneous assertion about the digital twin, but as a shorthand whose intended subject can be identified from the modelling context.

This approach depends on the possibility of resolving the shorthand without ambiguity. Some operational statements can be attributed to the heritage entity through straightforward mappings, while others concern the digital twin itself, its documentation, or the processes through which knowledge was produced. Such transformations require documented rules and, where their interpretation is not mechanically determined, appropriate evidence and review. They should not be assumed to be automatically reversible or lossless for every Wikibase statement. Within a defined interoperability profile, however, semantic projection can preserve the relevant identities and meanings while making explicit relationships that remain implicit in the operational application.

The central principle is that *ontological distinctions need not correspond to separately maintained user-facing records*. A Wikibase item can function as a pragmatic shorthand for a more fully articulated HDT-O representation, provided that the underlying distinctions can be reconstructed reliably. Wikibase and Betwixt provide operational environments for maintaining and reviewing knowledge, while semantic projection makes the relevant `HC1` and `HC2` resources, properties and relationships explicit for interoperability.

We believe that our approach reduces rather than introduces confusion for researchers, educators and data stewards. A textile researcher or ethnographer understands that, when working with our Wikibase, Sampo or Betwixt interface, they are not interacting with the physical sash located in the living room of the farmhouse. The digital twin is a volatile digital environment in which we investigate the `HC1` heritage entity indirectly through its `HC2` representation. For ontologists and data engineers, however, it is essential that we can provide an ontologically explicit account distinguishing the farmhouse, its living room and the sash from the digital environment in which they are represented and investigated.

The following worked example develops this approach using the Dēliņi farmhouse, its photographic documentation and persistent proposition sets, with the native Wikibase RDF, intermediate representation and HDT-O projection provided as separate Turtle files.

Let's try to talk briefer. So HC16 is derived from HC15 but must be expressed in formal language of knowledge representation. That qualifies to parts of our Wikidata items serialised in RDF. However, HC15 is not there yet. So, in a very brief, expalin to me the possible classification of the abstract Oblique photo, its ORF file, and three different manifestation each with an ISCC-instance and ISCC-data identifier derived from the bit-by-bit inspection of the manifestaiton I would distinguish five resources: one photographic work, one RAW original, and three derived manifestations.

Resource

Identity

crm:E36 Visual Item; provisionally HC1

Intellectual identity, independent of file format

Each of the four files can have its own ISCC-INSTANCE and ISCC-DATA identifiers, calculated from its digital content. These identify properties of the files, not the abstract photograph. ISCC-INSTANCE identifies the exact file bytes; ISCC-DATA is content-derived but should not be treated as an exact byte-for-byte identity test.

Three important distinctions:

HC15 identifies persistent digital objects, not necessarily knowledge representations. An ORF or JPEG can qualify.

HC16 specialises HC15 for persistent proposition sets. A formally expressed RDF proposition set can qualify, but an arbitrary RDF serialisation is not automatically an HC16.

HC1/HC2 concern the photographic work and its digital twin, if we provisionally treat the photograph as heritage. They do not need to be assigned to each file manifestation.

Thus, one photographic work can have multiple HC15 manifestations, each independently identifiable, while retaining a single intellectual identity and potentially a single HC2 digital twin.

The remaining modelling question is the precise property connecting those manifestations to the abstract photographic work.

What is the relationship between HC7 and HC15. What is the pro and con of a dual classification? In HDT-O, HC7 and HC15 are two classifications along different dimensions, not subclasses of one another.

HC7 Digital Audiovisual Object describes what the digital object represents: visual or audiovisual content.

HC15 Persistent Digital Object describes how its identity is fixed: complete bit-level content established at a particular creation moment.

Both descend from crmdig:D1 Digital Object, but through different branches. HDT-O does not declare them disjoint.

Dual classification of oblique_view.jpg ex:oblique-jpeg a hdt:HC7, hdt:HC15 . Advantages

Disadvantages

Captures visual content and bit-level persistence simultaneously

Combines representation-level and file-level identity

No additional resource or relationship needed

Can become awkward when one image has multiple renditions

Each manifestation can have its own ISCC identifiers

Queries about HC7 may return individual files rather than distinct visual works

Simple and compatible with the stated class hierarchy

Requires care when attaching rights, authorship and provenance

My recommendation Use dual classification for each fixed ORF, TIFF or JPEG file, but maintain a separate crm:E36 Visual Item for the abstract photograph.

This gives you three clearly distinguishable levels:

E36 — the photographic work, independent of encoding.

HC7 + HC15 — each persistent digital manifestation.

ISCC identifiers — evidence for the identity and content of each manifestation.

I would introduce separate HC7 and HC15 resources only if we need to model a digital visual representation that persists conceptually across several file versions. Otherwise, that extra distinction adds complexity without much benefit.

The digital twin is a volatile digital environment in which we investigate the HC1 heritage entity indirectly through its HC2 representation. For ontologists and data engineers, however, it is essential that we can provide an ontologically explicit account distinguishing the farmhouse, its living room and the sash

… I think the argument is coherent, but it currently combines three different questions that should be separated before we write the section:

How we store and distribute media, including access restrictions.

How we classify photographs as documentary works and potentially as heritage entities.

How we identify individual digital files within an evolving digital twin.

The strongest way to present this is to move from practical implementation to ontological interpretation.

1.  Media distribution and access governance Our Wikibase is not exclusively a graph of textual statements. It also provides access to photographs, sound recordings, videos and other digital resources.

We use Wikimedia Commons, and where possible Europeana, for material that can be openly distributed under appropriate licences, such as CC BY or CC BY-SA. Other media are maintained through the local Wikibase media extension or alternative access arrangements.

The reason is not simply copyright. A resource may involve several overlapping legal and ethical considerations: copyright, neighbouring rights, personality rights, privacy, consent and culturally sensitive information. A single Creative Commons licence may not adequately express all these conditions.

Important distinction: A media file can be linked to a knowledge graph without its digital content being represented as an independently identified graph resource. We should distinguish the presence of a media attachment from the explicit semantic modelling of that attachment.

I would avoid saying that the graph is multimodal only when files are directly represented as nodes. The system is multimodal in either case; the difference is the depth of semantic integration.

2.  Two different photographic situations I agree with your distinction between two types of photographs, but would formulate it slightly differently.

Type

What is being documented?

Example

Reproduction photograph

An existing documentary or heritage object

Digital reproduction of a historical photographic print

Documentary photograph

A heritage entity in a particular condition, place or moment

Photograph of the Dēliņi farmhouse in 2025

In the first case, we must distinguish the historical photograph as a work, its physical carrier (such as a photographic print), and its digital reproduction.

In the second case, the new photograph is itself a documentary work that represents the farmhouse.

Both situations may involve a photographic work, digital manifestations, rights, provenance and subsequent scholarly interpretation.

3.  Why give contemporary photographs their own digital twins? This is your most interesting argument, and I think it deserves emphasis.

You are proposing that photographs should not be treated merely as passive attachments to the farmhouse's digital twin. They can be independently identifiable objects of investigation.

For example, a photograph of the farmhouse taken in its original location, a photograph taken after reconstruction in the open-air museum, and a photograph taken during an inspection in 2026 have different documentary contexts.

Each may acquire additional knowledge concerning its date, authorship, depicted structures, historical interpretation, authenticity and rights.

Therefore, maintaining a digital twin of the photographic work has a practical justification: the knowledge about the photograph evolves independently of the knowledge about the farmhouse.

However, there is one terminological issue.

HC1 is specifically a Heritage Entity. It is not simply a general class for any independently identifiable intellectual work.

Your proposal is therefore not merely to maintain digital twins for photographs. It is also to treat contemporary heritage documentation as part of the heritage record, regardless of whether an individual photograph has independently acquired historical significance.

That is a defensible curatorial position, but I would present it explicitly as our proposed interpretation of heritage documentation, rather than as an established requirement of HDT-O or European museum practice.

The historical photographs and the 2025–2026 documentation can then all have HC1/HC2 pairs, but for reasons grounded in their documentary role, not because their heritage significance is necessarily identical.

4.  The separate role of HC7 and HC15 This is where I would be particularly precise.

The HC1/HC2 pair identifies the photographic work as an object of investigation and its evolving digital twin.

The HC7/HC15 dual classification identifies a particular fixed digital manifestation.

This allows one photographic work to have an ORF original, a TIFF preservation copy and several JPEG derivatives, each with its own ISCC identifiers.

The key is that the digital twin is volatile, but the individual file manifestations are persistent. They are not persistent because they belong to the twin; their persistence is a property of their fixed digital content.

HC7 and HC15 describe two independent aspects of that same digital object:

HC7: its role as a digital visual or audiovisual representation.

HC15: its identity as a fixed digital object.

This is a stronger explanation than describing HC15 simply as fixing identity within the digital twin.

5.  Suggested structure for the new section I would call it “Multimodal resources and persistent digital representations” and organise it into four short paragraphs:

Distribution and access: Wikimedia Commons, Europeana, local media and rights-sensitive access.

Photographs as documentary works: reproductions of existing records versus new documentation of heritage entities.

Photographs as objects of investigation: why the photographic works themselves can have HC1/HC2 identities, including contemporary documentation.

Persistent manifestations: HC7/HC15, ORF/JPEG/TIFF files and their ISCC identifiers.

One point I would not claim without qualification is that European museum practice requires contemporary object photographs to be recognised as heritage entities. The stronger, more supportable claim is that our model treats them as integral documentary components of the heritage record, whose independent provenance, rights and evolving interpretation justify their own digital twins.

That gives you a coherent argument without conflating heritage status, documentary identity, digital representation and bit-level persistence.
